title: Area Worksheets: Counting Square Units
intro: Area tells how much surface a shape covers. Count the equal squares inside the shape, not the lines around it.
html:
One square is one square unit

Imagine covering a tabletop with equal square tiles. If the tiles leave no gaps and do not overlap, their total number tells how many square units the surface covers. In these grids, every small tile represents one square unit.

3 rows of 4 squares cover 12 square units.

Count each square once, or add the rows: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.

Count spaces, not grid lines

Point inside a square as you count it. The boundary lines separate tiles; they are not extra tiles. Work across one row, then move to the next row so you do not skip or count a square twice.

If the child counts only the outside squares: ask whether the middle squares also cover part of the surface. Area includes every square inside the shape.

Use equal rows

Each row of a rectangular grid has the same number of squares. Once you know there are four squares in one row and three rows, you can use 3 × 4 = 12. Explain what each factor counts before relying on the multiplication fact.

One row still has area

A single row of five square tiles covers five square units. A single tile covers one square unit. A grid does not need several rows to have area.

Keep the unit with the answer

Write “12 square units” for the three-by-four grid. The worksheet supplies the unit beside the answer box. A length around the outside would be a perimeter in units, which answers a different question.

Changing the arrangement

Arrange twelve physical square tiles in three rows of four, then in two rows of six. Both arrangements cover twelve square units when there are no gaps or overlaps. The boundary can change even though the number of tiles stays the same.

About this practice

Each set has six distinct rectangular grids with one to five rows and one to five columns. All tiles are whole squares. Count them or use equal rows; the answer key gives the total area. Use the working space to show a repeated sum or multiplication equation.

The drawings may appear at different sizes on different screens. Each displayed tile still represents one square unit; do not measure it with a ruler. Partial squares, irregular shapes, and unknown side lengths are not included.
